entries.title: PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase
entries.summary: PostgreSQL 19 reached GA today and it's already available on Lakebase. New major...
entries.content:
Try the new features: REPACK, query plan advice, WAIT FOR LSN, and more

  • PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase the same day the community released it. To try it, create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19.
  • This PostgreSQL release focuses on operational control. REPACK reclaims space while reads and writes continue, query plan advice lets you stabilize plans that go wrong, and WAIT FOR LSN gives you read-your-writes on replicas. Logical replication also gets several upgrades.
  • Several Lakebase engineers are PostgreSQL committers and contributors who worked on this release, from query plan advice to shared memory and release management.

PostgreSQL 19 reached GA today and it's already available on Lakebase. New major versions often take weeks to reach other managed PostgreSQL services. Instead, we wanted to give access to it to our customers the same day.

Several engineers on the Lakebase team are PostgreSQL committers and contributors, and they worked on this release directly, from query plan advice to shared memory, locale handling, and release management. To try it, create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19 as the version.

PostgreSQL 19 is a practical release. There is no single headline feature that changes what PostgreSQL is. Instead, version 19 goes after operational problems that database teams know well: bloated tables, unstable query plans, replica lag, incomplete statistics, and maintenance work that is hard to run safely in production.

The common thread is control. PostgreSQL 19 gives you more ways to step in when the defaults are not enough, without giving up the project's bias toward reliability and predictable behavior.

The full list of changes is in the PostgreSQL 19 release notes.

PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control, so an 

UPDATE
creates a new row version and a 
DELETE
leaves a dead tuple behind. Routine vacuuming makes that space reusable, but it doesn't necessarily return space to the operating system or restore a useful physical row order. Over time, heavily updated tables can become bloated and poorly clustered.

The usual fixes have been 

VACUUM FULL
, 
CLUSTER
, or external tools such as 
pg_repack
. The built-in commands work, but they take an 
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
lock for the whole operation, blocking normal access to the table.

PostgreSQL 19 adds 

REPACK
, which reclaims space while normal reads and writes continue during most of the operation. For example, a chat application can rebuild its 
messages
table while clustering rows by conversation and send time using an existing index: 

REPACK
reclaims space like 
VACUUM FULL
; with 
USING INDEX
, it also physically orders rows like 
CLUSTER
. With 
CONCURRENTLY
, PostgreSQL rebuilds the table while normal reads and writes continue, capturing ongoing changes through logical decoding. It then takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to apply any remaining captured changes and swap the new table and index files into place. This phase is typically brief but can take longer on a busy table.

There are operational constraints. Concurrent repacking creates an additional replication slot for the duration of the operation, so it needs free capacity under 

max_repack_replication_slots
and a table with either a non-deferrable primary key or a suitable index-based replica identity. It also needs temporary disk space for a copy of the table and all its indexes, potentially plus a sort file up to the size of the table. Tables with heavy update and delete traffic face an additional limit: the current upstream PostgreSQL 19 implementation fails if more than about 104 million tuples in the target table are updated or deleted while 
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY)
is running. This counts changes made during the repack, not rows already in the table.

Not every relation type is eligible. Long-running transactions can delay the final lock. Concurrent repacking is also not MVCC-safe: after it commits, transactions using snapshots taken before the repack began can see the table as empty. Physical clustering also degrades as later writes arrive.

REPACK CONCURRENTLY
still needs planning, but it brings into core a job that previously required more downtime or an extension.

The PostgreSQL cost-based optimizer uses table statistics and cost estimates to choose an execution plan. Most of the time, that works well.

Statistics describe individual tables well, but real datasets often contain relationships that are harder to capture. Imagine that enterprise customers make up 0.1% of customers but generate 30% of orders. Per-table statistics cannot capture that cross-table correlation.

With an index on 

orders.customer_id,
the planner may estimate that each enterprise customer has only a few orders and choose a nested loop that repeatedly probes the index. If those customers actually account for 30% of orders, each lookup returns far more rows than expected, and a hash join may be more appropriate.

PostgreSQL 19 adds 

pg_plan_advice
and 
pg_stash_advice
for these situations: 
  • pg_plan_advice
    describes planner decisions as advice, applies supplied advice, and reports whether it was followed.
  • pg_stash_advice
    stores advice by query ID and applies it automatically when a matching query is planned

These components do not add cross-table statistics or replace the planner. Instead, they let you intervene when an inaccurate estimate produces a poor plan.

Consider a query that counts orders from enterprise customers:

Here, 

c
is the alias for the filtered customers table. The following advice asks PostgreSQL to place those customers on the inner side of a hash join:

When PostgreSQL can apply the advice, 

EXPLAIN
reports feedback similar to: 

matched
means the resulting plan complies with the advice. It does not mean the new plan is necessarily better; you still need to evaluate it against the actual workload.

Unlike inline optimizer hints, plan advice lives outside the application’s query text. You can inspect the current plan, test focused advice, and then stash it by query ID.

pg_stash_advice
is the component that applies stashed advice automatically. Create the extension in each database before using its stash-management functions:

Create a stash and associate the tested advice with the query ID reported by 

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE)
. Replace 
with the identifier from your plan:

Configure the database to use the stash for new connections:

Replace 

appdb
with the name of your database.

Treat plan advice as a stabilizer once you've diagnosed the problem. Data distributions change, cached prepared statements may keep using an older plan for a while, and the optimizer is still right more often than it is wrong.

When the planner unexpectedly switches a critical query to a worse plan, PostgreSQL 19 gives you a supported way to stabilize it.

Autovacuum can now use parallel workers when vacuuming indexes, controlled by 

autovacuum_max_parallel_workers
.  A new scoring system prioritizes eligible tables based on how urgently they need vacuuming or analysis.

New statistics views expose more of what the server is doing:

  • pg_stat_lock
    reports statistics by lock type.
  • pg_stat_recovery
    shows recovery status.
  • pg_stat_autovacuum_scores
    shows how autovacuum prioritizes tables.

Query-level diagnostics improve as well. 

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, IO)
reports asynchronous I/O activity, and 
auto_explain.log_io
can include the same information in logged plans.

PostgreSQL 19 also reports bytes written for full-page images in 

pg_stat_wal
, 
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL)
, and vacuum and analyze logs.

Together, these make performance investigations less dependent on inference. You can see why maintenance work was prioritized, where asynchronous I/O happened, and how many WAL bytes came from full-page images.

Logical replication has become core infrastructure for change data capture, migrations, real-time serving, and ETL pipelines. PostgreSQL 19 closes several long-standing gaps:

  • Logical decoding can be activated without a restart when 
    wal_level
    is 
    replica
    . Creating the first valid logical replication slot raises 
    effective_wal_level
    to 
    logical
    , showing the WAL level currently in effect.
  • Sequence values can be synchronized from publishers to subscribers.
  • Publications can include all sequences with 
    FOR ALL SEQUENCES
    .
  • CREATE PUBLICATION ... FOR ALL TABLES EXCEPT (...)
    publishes all tables except a named set.
  • Subscriptions can reuse connection details from a 
    postgres_fdw
    server with 
    CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER
    .
  • The 
    retain_dead_tuples
    subscription option preserves enough information to 
    detect update_deleted
    conflicts, where a replicated update targets a row deleted by another origin. Detection also requires 
    track_commit_timestamp
    on the subscriber, and 
    pg_stat_subscription_stats
    counts these conflicts.

Sequence synchronization removes an awkward migration edge case, especially during major-version upgrades that use logical replication. Copying table rows without advancing their sequences can leave a promoted subscriber generating values that already exist, causing duplicate-key errors.

PostgreSQL copies the initial sequence values when the subscription is created with 

copy_data = true
, the default. Later sequence changes are not streamed continuously, so refresh them immediately before cutover:

This updates the sequences already known to the subscription to their current values on the publisher. If the publication has gained new sequences, use 

ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH
PUBLICATION
to add them and synchronize their values before cutover.

Asynchronous read replicas add read capacity without making primary commits wait for them. The tradeoff is replication lag. An application can commit a write on the primary, immediately read from a replica, and not find the row because the replica has not replayed the relevant WAL yet.

PostgreSQL 19 adds a direct way to coordinate that handoff. An LSN identifies a position in the PostgreSQL WAL, and

 WAIT FOR LSN
blocks the standby until replay reaches at least the requested position:

By default, 

WAIT FOR LSN
waits indefinitely for the standby to replay the requested LSN. Other modes can wait for WAL to be written or flushed, and you can set a timeout.

The client or connection pooler still has to carry the LSN from the primary to the replica. The database now provides the missing synchronization step, so read-your-writes behavior no longer needs polling or arbitrary sleeps.

Foreign data wrappers let PostgreSQL query remote systems as if their data were local. Planning those queries has always been hard when the local optimizer does not know the remote table’s size or data distribution.

PostgreSQL 19 lets 

postgres_fdw
import statistics from the remote server: 

ANALYZE
imports the existing remote statistics into the local server. If the import fails, 
postgres_fdw
falls back to row sampling. The remote statistics therefore need to be current.

Without remote statistics, PostgreSQL may rely on fallback size estimates and choose a nested loop. After importing them, the planner can estimate row counts more accurately and may choose a hash join instead.

Federated queries still pay network and remote-system costs, but accurate row estimates remove a major source of avoidable bad plans.

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT
gives you a clean get-or-create pattern that returns both existing and newly inserted rows:

It replaces the 

DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col
workaround, which performs an update even though no values change. That creates a new row version and leaves a dead tuple on every conflict. 

COPY TO
can now emit JSON directly. By default, it writes one object per line, while 
FORCE_ARRAY
wraps the output in a single JSON array:

The new JSON format is export-only, so 

COPY FROM
does not accept it.

Lastly, a few compact changes with a quality-of-life payoff:

  • JSON path expressions gain familiar string methods such as 
    btrim()
    , 
    lower()
    , 
    replace()
    , and 
    split_part()
    .
  • The 
    random(min, max)
    family now supports 
    date
    , 
    timestamp
    , and 
    timestamptz
    , which helps with tests and synthetic datasets.
  • Five window functions accept 
    IGNORE NULLS
    and
     RESPECT NULLS
    .
  • When 
    io_method = worker
    , I/O workers scale automatically between 
    io_min_workers
    and 
    io_max_workers
    . Foreign-key checks are faster, and the planner and executor get another round of targeted optimizations.

Several major features landed during PostgreSQL 19 development but were removed before release. Reviewers found correctness or design problems that were too risky to resolve late in the cycle, so the community held the features for a later release.

Some of the features that finally won't ship in 19:

  • SQL/PGQ
    property graph queries. 
    CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH
    and 
    GRAPH_TABLE
    brought graph pattern matching over regular tables into SQL. Reverted on September 7, 2026.
  • UPDATE and DELETE ... FOR PORTION OF.
    Temporal updates and deletes that split rows to preserve history outside the targeted time range.  Reverted on September 15, 2026.
  • ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS
    and 
    SPLIT PARTITION
    . Built-in commands for combining or dividing partitions. Reverted on August 27, 2026.
  • GROUP BY ALL
    . Shorthand for grouping by every non-aggregate expression in the select list.. Reverted on July 17, 2026.
  • Non-text output formats for 
    pg_dumpall
    .  Reverted on June 18, 2026.
  • DDL extraction functions. 
    pg_get_role_ddl()
    , 
    pg_get_tablespace_ddl()
    , and 
    pg_get_database_ddl()
    were Reverted on September 13, 2026.

PostgreSQL is made by its contributors: thank you to the hundreds of community contributors credited in the release notes. Special thanks to the engineers on the Lakebase team who worked on this version of PostgreSQL: 

  • Robert Haas  wrote pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice (the latter with Lukas Fittl)
  • Heikki Linnakangas  worked on a new mechanism for registering shared memory, a rework of how subsystems allocate it, multixact fixes, and the new default of 128 for max_locks_per_transaction
  • Jeff Davis  wrote the change that lets CREATE SUBSCRIPTION reuse a postgres_fdw server's connection details, and did a long run of locale and character-handling work
  • Jonathan Katz worked on the PostgreSQL 19 press release and handled release shepherding
  • Matthias van de Meent worked on multiple commits including the change to static index access method routines
  • Alexander Lakhin found and reported multiple bugs

As with any new major version of PostgreSQL, we recommend a measured approach to adopting it. Before moving production workloads to 19.0, we suggest you:

  • Test your own workloads, queries, and extensions on PostgreSQL 19 in a development or staging environment first
  • Compare performance and behavior against your current version, since major releases can change query plans and defaults
  • Check that the extensions you rely on are available on PostgreSQL 19 (see below).
  • Keep production on your current version until you're comfortable with the results

PostgreSQL19 also changes several defaults and compatibility behaviors. Check these before you upgrade:

  • JIT compilation is off by default
  • TOAST compression defaults to LZ4 instead of pglz
  • MD5 password authentication emits stronger deprecation warnings
  • RADIUS authentication support is removed
  • standard_conforming_strings is always on
  • pg_upgrade rejects clusters with affected btree_gist indexes on inet or cidr
  • Database, role, and tablespace names can no longer contain carriage returns or line feeds

We've covered most of the extensions supported in our PostgreSQL 18 release, but not all of them are available on PostgreSQL 19 yet. We're adding more as they become available from the extension providers. If your workload depends on a specific extension, confirm it's available on PostgreSQL 19 before you plan a migration.

The community typically ships its first minor release a few months after a major version, as real-world usage surfaces fixes and refinements. PostgreSQL 19.1 is anticipated in February, and many teams plan production upgrades around that release. That's a common and sensible pattern for any .0 release, and it's just as true here.

Whatever your timeline, we're here to help. If you'd like to talk through upgrade planning or testing, reach out to your account team or Databricks support.

PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase today. Create a PostgreSQL 19 project in your workspace to try it, or get started with Lakebase if you're new to it.

entries.title: Introducing CustomerLake Conversions: Improve advertising performance with first-party customer context
entries.summary: Two purchases can look identical in campaign reports and mean very different things to your business...
entries.content:
Show advertising platforms which conversions are the most valuable, then bring campaign results back to your customer data and AI foundation, with full control over what you share.

by Tasso Argyros, Katy Yuan and Cindy Jiang

  • CustomerLake Conversions is a new capability of CustomerLake Campaign Agents, the Agentic CDP built natively in Databricks. It connects first-party customer data and ML models to advertising activation and measurement.
  • Marketers define value-based conversion signals, such as a first purchase from a customer with high predicted lifetime value, then send those signals and audiences to ad platforms through Conversions API (CAPI) integrations. Campaign performance insights return to Databricks via OpenSharing and Lakeflow Connect.
  • Brands and agencies work from one governed foundation in Unity Catalog, with delegated permissions and an audit trail of what was sent where. Launch partners include Amazon Ads, Google, LinkedIn, Meta, Microsoft Ads, Reddit, Snapchat, The Trade Desk, Tiktok, Epsilon, Merkle, and Omnicom.

Two purchases can look identical in campaign reports and mean very different things to your business. One buyer has potential to become a loyal regular; the other is a first-time purchase driven by a deep discount. Both count as conversions, but their long-term value can be very different.

Your business has data that helps identify the difference: purchase history, margin, loyalty, engagement, and predicted lifetime value. Bringing that understanding into advertising can change the customers you pursue, the signals you send, and how you evaluate success.

Today, we’re introducing CustomerLake Conversions: a new capability within Databricks’ Agentic CDP that connects first-party data and context directly to advertising activation and measurement. It helps brands pursue more valuable conversions and improve return on ad spend (ROAS), while controlling the data they share.

When available, CustomerLake Conversions will be accessible to all customers using Campaign Agents in CustomerLake.

We’re proud to collaborate with these advertising and agency partners for this launch:

CustomerLake is the Agentic CDP built natively in Databricks, the enterprise data and AI platform where your most complete customer context already lives. Its Campaign Agents help marketers build audiences in natural language, activate across channels, and power 1:1 personalized experiences.

CustomerLake Conversions extends Campaign Agents to advertising performance by connecting three steps directly on your trusted foundation:

  • Define what matters. Use first-party data and ML models to build audiences and identify meaningful conversion signals, such as a qualified lead or a first purchase from a customer predicted to be high value.
  • Activate across paid media. Audience and Conversions API (CAPI) integrations deliver selected audiences and conversion signals, through native Reverse ETL connectors, to advertising platforms.
  • Bring results back. OpenSharing integrations and Lakeflow Connect bring campaign insights back into Databricks, where teams can evaluate advertising performance alongside customer and business context.

The dedicated Conversions tab within CustomerLake Campaign Agents lets marketers select conversion data, configure destinations, and manage delivery within the Campaign Agents workflow.

Together, these capabilities connect the intelligence behind your targeting, the signals sent to platforms, and the results used to guide future investment.

As advertising platforms automate more bidding, targeting, and campaign decisions, the only lever advertisers fully control is what signals they feed them. That puts a premium on first-party data, and on the business context that explains what it means.

However, getting richer business context into paid media often requires manual data extracts, custom integrations, and handoffs across marketing, analytics, engineering, and agency teams. Audiences can diverge across platforms, and campaign reporting is delayed and disconnected from customer and revenue data.

That means attribution is fuzzy, acquisition costs creep up, and teams can't say with confidence which paid channels are converting and which aren’t.

CustomerLake Conversions brings signal creation and activation to where customer data and models already live. A retailer can use predicted lifetime value to rapidly adjust lookalike targeting. A B2B company can use qualified leads or closed won revenue to represent progress beyond a submitted form. Marketers still define success; CustomerLake helps translate those priorities into signals advertising platforms can use.

Let’s consider a retailer whose goal is to acquire more customers who are likely to buy again.

Before: The retailer sends purchase events and order values to its advertising platforms, while its lifetime value model lives in the data platform, maintained by the data team. Using that model in paid media requires data extracts, platform-specific uploads, and separate delivery workflows. Their agency then reconciles campaign reports with revenue data to evaluate acquisition quality.

With CustomerLake Conversions: The paid media team uses its existing lifetime value model in Databricks to identify completed first purchases from customers likely to become repeat buyers. In the Conversions tab, the team configures delivery of those purchase events to supported advertising platforms through CAPI. The same customer data can also inform the audiences the team builds and syncs.

Campaign insights flow back into Databricks, where the retailer and its agency evaluate acquisition spend alongside customer value. They can refine audiences, signals, and media strategy using the same customer and business context that informed activation.

The result? The ad platform can better optimize what a good customer looks like. The retailer gets a faster, clearer view of which campaigns acquire the customers it wants to grow with.

For many enterprises, agencies provide core strategy, identity assets, models, and media expertise that turn customer intelligence into performance.

CustomerLake Conversions gives brands and agencies a shared foundation for that work. Agencies get governed access to customer context in the lakehouse, without copying or duplicating data. The brand controls what is shared and with whom, and the agency does its best work on better data. In practice, what this could look like:

  • Configure delivery. Agencies can set up destinations and conversion definitions in the client's CustomerLake Conversions tab, using permissions the brand delegates, with an audit trail of what was sent where.
  • Apply unique intelligence. Agencies can combine their identity data and predictive models, such as lifetime value and propensity scores, with a brand’s first-party data to build more relevant audiences and conversion signals. For example, Epsilon’s identity graph can connect conversion events to customer identities even when the original event has limited identifying information. Adding those identifiers to the data sent via CAPI can help ad platforms match more conversions, giving advertisers a fuller picture of how their campaigns perform and giving platforms more signals to optimize delivery.
  • Measure results. Campaign insights from the platforms feed the agency's MMM and incrementality studies.

The brand brings customer understanding. The agency brings its expertise in reaching and engaging them. CustomerLake connects both to activation.

Activating richer customer context requires clear control over its use. CustomerLake Conversions is designed so customers own their data and stay in control:

  • Your data stays governed. Customer profiles and business context are secured and governed by Unity Catalog.
  • You choose the destinations. You decide which audiences and conversion events go to which platforms.
  • You can see what was sent. An audit trail provides visibility into what was sent and where.
  • Humans stay in the loop. Your team sets the strategy, goals and guardrails. Agents help scale execution.

Today, campaigns outlive the assumptions they launched with. A single campaign can take 6+ teams and 60+ days to launch. By then, customers have moved on.

CustomerLake enables a continuous operating model, where each customer interaction helps inform the next decision. As campaign results feed back into the same Data + AI foundation, agents can help marketers and agencies recognize changes, recommend adjustments, and keep activation aligned with business goals. People define what matters, set the strategy, and establish the guardrails; agents help execution keep pace with customer demand.

CustomerLake Conversions brings paid media into the broader vision of Infinity Campaigns: continuous engagement that learns and adapts as customer context changes. It advances our mission of marketing in context: turning everything you know about your customers into growth.

To get started with CustomerLake Conversions, contact your Databricks account team.
